{{Short description|Special case in probability theory; introduces tail events}}
{{Redirect|Tail event|"tail events" meaning "rare events"|fat tail}}

In [[probability theory]], '''Kolmogorov's zero–one law''', named in honor of [[Andrey Nikolaevich Kolmogorov]], specifies that a certain type of [[Event (probability theory)|event]], namely a ''tail event of independent [[sigma-algebra|&sigma;-algebras]]'', will either [[almost surely]] happen or almost surely not happen; that is, the [[probability]] of such an event occurring is zero or one.

Tail events are defined in terms of [[Countable set|countably infinite]] families of &sigma;-algebras. For illustrative purposes, we present here the special case in which each sigma algebra is generated by a [[random variable]] <math>X_k</math> for <math>k\in\mathbb N</math>. Let <math>\mathcal{F}</math> be the sigma-algebra generated jointly by all of the <math>X_k</math>. Then, a '''tail event''' <math>F \in \mathcal{F}</math> is an event the occurrence of which cannot depend on the outcome of a finite subfamily of these random variables. (Note: <math>F</math> belonging to <math>\mathcal{F}</math> implies that membership in <math>F</math> is uniquely determined by the values of the <math>X_k</math>, but the latter condition is strictly weaker and does not suffice to prove the zero-one law.) For example, the event that the sequence of the <math>X_k</math> [[Convergence of random variables|converges]], and the event that its sum converges are both tail events. If the <math>X_k</math> are, for example, all [[Bernoulli distribution|Bernoulli-distributed]], then the event that there are infinitely many <math>k\in\mathbb N</math> such that <math>X_k=X_{k+1}=\dots=X_{k+100}=1</math> is a tail event. If each <math>X_k</math> models the outcome of the <math>k^{th}</math> coin toss in a modeled, infinite sequence of coin tosses, this means that a sequence of 100 consecutive heads occurring infinitely many times is a tail event in this model.

Tail events are precisely those events whose occurrence can still be determined if an arbitrarily large but finite initial segment of the <math>X_k</math> is removed.

In many situations, it can be easy to apply Kolmogorov's zero–one law to show that some event has probability 0 or 1, but surprisingly hard to determine ''which'' of these two extreme values is the correct one.

== Formulation ==
A more general statement of Kolmogorov's zero–one law holds for sequences of independent &sigma;-algebras. Let <math>(\Omega, F, P)</math> be a [[probability space]] and let <math>F_n</math> be a sequence of &sigma;-algebras contained in <math>F</math>. Let
:<math>G_n=\sigma\bigg(\bigcup_{k=n}^\infty F_k\bigg)</math>
be the smallest <math>\sigma</math>-algebra containing <math>F_n, F_{n+1}, ...</math>. Then the ''terminal <math>\sigma</math>-algebra'' of the <math>F_n</math> is defined as <math>\mathcal T((F_n)_{n\in\mathbb N})=\bigcap_{n=1}^\infty G_n</math>.

Kolmogorov's zero–one law asserts that, if the ''<math>F_n</math>'' are [[stochastically independent]], then for any event <math>E\in \mathcal T((F_n)_{n\in\mathbb N})</math>, one has either <math>P(E) = 0</math> or <math>P(E) = 1</math>.

The statement of the law in terms of random variables is obtained from the latter by taking each ''<math>F_n</math>'' to be the &sigma;-algebra generated by the random variable <math>X_n</math>. A tail event is then by definition an event which is [[Measure (mathematics)|measurable]] with respect to the &sigma;-algebra generated by all ''<math>X_n</math>,'' but which is [[Independence (probability theory)|independent]] of any finite number of ''<math>X_n</math>.'' That is, a tail event is precisely an element of the terminal &sigma;-algebra <math>\textstyle{\bigcap_{n=1}^\infty G_n}</math>.

==Examples==

# Let <math>(X,\mathcal{B},\mu)</math> be a [[standard probability space]], and let <math>T</math> be an invertible, [[measure-preserving transformation]]. Then <math>T</math> is called a [[Kolmogorov automorphism]] or ''K''-automorphism, ''K''-transform or ''K''-shift, if there exists a sub-[[sigma algebra]] <math>\mathcal{K} \sub \mathcal{B}</math> such that the following three properties hold: <math display="block">\mbox{(1) }\mathcal{K}\subset T\mathcal{K} 
</math><math display="block">\mbox{(2) }\bigvee_{n=0}^\infty T^n \mathcal{K}=\mathcal{B}</math><math display="block">\mbox{(3) }\bigcap_{n=0}^\infty T^{-n} \mathcal{K} = \{X,\varnothing\}</math> Here, the symbol <math>\or</math> is the [[Join (sigma algebra)|join of sigma algebras]], while <math>\cap</math> is [[set intersection]]. The equality should be understood as holding [[almost everywhere]], that is, differing at most on a set of [[measure zero]].  A ''K''-automorphism by construction necessarily obeys Kolmogorov's 0-1 Law. It can be further shown that all [[Bernoulli automorphism|Bernoulli automorphisms]] are ''K''-automorphisms, but not ''vice versa''.
# The presence of an infinite cluster in the context of [[percolation theory]] also obeys the 0-1 law. 
# Let <math>\{X_n\}_n</math> be a sequence of independent random variables, then the event <math>E</math> defined below is a tail event: <math display="block">E = \left\{\lim _{n \rightarrow \infty} \sum_{k=1}^n X_k \text { exists }\right\}</math>Thus by Kolmogorov's 0-1 law, it has either probability 0 or 1 to happen. Note that independence is required for the tail event condition to hold. Without independence we can consider a sequence that's either <math>(0,0,0,\dots)</math> or <math>(1,1,1,\dots)</math> with probability <math>\frac{1}{2}</math> each. In this case the sum converges with probability <math>\frac{1}{2}</math>.

== Possible confusion with fat tails ==
The "tail events" in the Kolmogorov zero-one law are not related to the "tail events" in the sense of [[Fat-tailed distribution|fat-tailed distributions]] (or the closely related [[Long tail|long tails]] and [[Tail risk|tail risks]]). The events we consider in this article are things like [[Convergent sequences|convergence/non-convergence of sequences]], while the latter type of event means something like "[[outliers]]".
